## Case

This proposal sets out the case for a water recycling plant and seeks support for taking the project forward. By way of background, the site currently takes the whole of its process water from the municipal supply and returns the whole of its effluent to the municipal sewer. An important consequence of this arrangement is that the site's water costs are effectively set twice over: a charge is incurred on the water that is drawn in, and a further charge is incurred on the water that is sent out, and both of these charges fall on water that passes through the process just once before being discarded. Alongside the question of cost, the arrangement also determines the site's exposure. Because the process holds no water supply of its own, any interruption or restriction affecting the municipal supply would reach production directly and without any buffer, while the terms of the discharge consent govern the stream of effluent leaving the site, a stream which the site has no practical ability to hold back.

It is against this background that the recycling proposal has been developed. A water recycling plant would treat the effluent on site and return the treated water to the process for reuse. The intake from the municipal supply would fall, the discharge to the municipal sewer would fall by the same recovered stream, and the process would gain a supply that sits under the site's own control. It is worth emphasising that the recovered water is not a by-product in search of a use: it would displace purchased water at precisely the point where the site already uses water, and it would relieve the discharge at precisely the point where the consent binds most tightly. The case for the plant is therefore a case about cost and security taken together — on the one hand the ongoing running cost of a single-use water system, and on the other hand the operational risk of depending on a supply and a discharge that both lie outside the site's control.

It should also be recognised that a proposal of this kind cannot by itself settle the questions on which a construction decision would have to rest. The treatment duty has to be fixed on the measured quality of the actual effluent, the treatment process has to be selected against that duty, and the plant has to be priced from vendor quotations rather than estimated from comparable installations elsewhere. All of that work belongs to detailed design, the stage at which a case of this kind is converted into a price. The scope that the design has to settle covers the whole path of the water: collection of the effluent as it leaves the process, equalisation so that the treatment stage sees a steady load rather than the swings of the producing process, the treatment stage itself, storage of the treated water, and return of that water to the points of use at the quality that each use requires. Which of those elements turns out to be large and which turns out to be small depends on the effluent and on the uses, and it is that dependence which leads this proposal to fix the scope by function and to leave the sizing of it to the design stage.

## Costs

Turning to the financial side of the proposal, the estimated capital cost of the water recycling plant is $400k. This figure is an estimate prepared at proposal stage, built up from the expected scope of the treatment plant and its installation, and it will in due course be replaced, during detailed design, by firm prices for the selected process and its equipment. The appraisal of the plant runs over a 7-year horizon, and the comparison that it makes is between two complete positions over that period: on one side, the cost of building and operating the recycling plant, and on the other side, the cost of continuing to take all process water from the municipal supply and to discharge all effluent to the municipal sewer.

A word is in order about the standing of the capital figure itself. An estimate made at proposal stage, before the process has been selected and before any vendor has priced the equipment, is a planning figure with a wide tolerance around it, and it is used in this proposal for one purpose only, namely to size the commitment that a construction decision would involve, so that the sequence of decisions is proportioned to the sum at stake. It is not a price and it is not a budget, and to treat it as either would be to overstate what is currently known. The appraisal has been constructed so as to absorb its replacement: when the firm price arrives from detailed design, the appraisal is simply rerun on that price, with no change required to its structure.

The operating costs of the plant, by contrast, are not yet fixed, and this proposal does not attempt to state them as figures. Energy for treatment and pumping, treatment consumables, maintenance of the treatment equipment and the labour of operating the plant all belong to the operating account, and each of them depends on the process that detailed design selects and on the duty that the measured quality of the effluent imposes. The savings side of the appraisal is open in much the same way: the value of the recovered water depends on the volume recovered and on the intake and discharge charges that it displaces, and the volume recovered is itself one of the results of the design. What can be stated at this stage is the structure of the appraisal and the term over which it runs. The appraisal period is 7 years from the start of operation, the capital figure under appraisal is the $400k estimated here and, in due course, the firm price that replaces it, and the decision that the appraisal exists to support is the construction decision rather than the decision sought in this proposal.

## Schedule

In terms of timing, work would start one quarter after approval. The first stage is detailed design itself, which comprises characterisation of the effluent by means of a sampling programme — the treatment duty has to rest on the effluent as it actually is, rather than on the effluent as it might be assumed to be — together with selection of the treatment process against the measured duty and pricing of the plant from vendor quotations for the selected process. Detailed design concludes with a firm capital price and a completed appraisal, and with the construction case stated on the basis of both.

Procurement, construction and commissioning then follow the design in that order. No contractor is named in this proposal, and none should be inferred from it: the construction contractor is to be appointed by competitive tender on the completed design, so that all of the tenders are priced against one and the same fixed scope. Commissioning returns the plant to the operating organisation with the quality of its treated water demonstrated against the duty that the design set. It should be noted that each stage following approval depends on the stage before it: procurement cannot be priced before the design has fixed the scope, and construction cannot be tendered before procurement has established the market. The schedule is therefore best understood as a sequence with one fixed point at its head — the start, one quarter after approval — and with the construction decision standing between detailed design and everything that is to follow it.

## Decision requested

It remains to state the decision that this proposal requests. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design for the water recycling plant. In the event of approval, the project team would proceed to detailed design, encompassing the effluent sampling programme, the selection of the treatment process and the firm pricing of the plant. Approval on this basis would commit the organisation to that design work and to nothing beyond it: it would not authorise construction, it would not commit the $400k of capital, and it would not select a contractor.

The construction decision would come back to the same point of decision once detailed design is complete, supported at that stage by the firm price and the completed appraisal in place of the estimate and the structure set out in this document. Should it turn out that the firm price or the appraisal does not support construction, the project would end at the design stage, leaving the site with its effluent characterised and its treatment options priced, information that retains its value either way. The request is accordingly a deliberately narrow one: to approve the stage that turns a proposal into a priced and appraised project, reserving the larger commitment until the evidence on which it should rest actually exists.
